cim: Fitbit Edge review: notable upgrade over the Charge 6 for GPS and heart rate, Google Health app is an improvement, but lacks software polish and NFC payments (Ray Maker/DC Rainmaker)
cim_eredeti: Fitbit Edge review: notable upgrade over the Charge 6 for GPS and heart rate, Google Health app is an improvement, but lacks software polish and NFC payments (Ray Maker/DC Rainmaker)
szoveg_eredeti:
The Fitbit Edge could most easily be called the Fitbit Charge 7, but sometimes switching things up is a good refresh for companies and brands, and so here we are. In many ways, the Fitbit Edge will feel very familiar to Fitbit Charge users, yet it’ll concurrently feel very much like a recent Google Pixel Watch. That’s both good and bad. There are a lot of good things coming from the Pixel Watch 5 & Fitbit Air that have landed here. Yet equally, having used it the past few weeks, there are a number of smaller things that aren’t quite what we had on the very popular Fitbit Charge series.

Speaking of which, both my wife and I have been using Fitbit Edge units over this last while on all of our workouts. Runs, rides, hikes, walks, gym stuff, and everything in between. With that, let’s dive into what’s new, and then all my daily and workout usage experiences.

The Fitbit Edge is the next version of the Fitbit Charge 6, which came out in 2023. Here’s how it’s different:

– Increased screen/display by 46% (has 1.34” display) – Case thickness is 11.5mm – Added physical side button that actually clicks (previous was just a touch area) – Added altimeter (for stair tracking, as well as elevation tracking) – Added automatic workout detection (now supports 100 sports) – Increased supported manual workout profiles to 50 workout profiles – Made user-replaceable/serviceable battery (the first Fitbit-branded product to do so) – GPS accuracy improvement claimed at 40% more accurate (via new GPS chipset, and new aluminum case design) – Switched to a more modern user interface, matching the Pixel Watch 5 series – Added structured workout support – Added support for dual usage with Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air (e.g., switching back and forth seamlessly) – Added fast charging (5 minutes gets you 1 day of usage) – Removed Google Pay (NFC Contactless payments) – Removed EDA Scan feature (but does have continuous stress monitoring in the background) – Changed the band attachment mechanism (old Fitbit habits die hard) – Switched the charger to the same charger as the Fitbit Air (hey, at least they picked something else they already had this time) – Added a bunch of band accessory types – Price increased to $179 (officially the Charge 6 was $159 previously, but realistically it sat between $99 and $129 virtually all the time) – Also a Stephen Curry model at $219 (US, Canada, EMEA)

In terms of some other general specs, just for recap purposes:

– Same claimed 7-day battery life – Still has heart rate broadcasting feature via Bluetooth (though it can be a bit funky in terms of compatibility) – Still has music control of your phone’s music (no onboard music storage) – Still has Google Maps turn-by-turn directions (with phone) – Still has smartphone notifications (more integration on Android than iOS) – Still has full sleep tracking – Still has continuous heart rate monitoring (background and workout) – Still supports high & low heart rate alerts – Supports the Google Health Guardian features announced a few months ago – You can do quick replies on Android, though not on iOS devices – Has FDA/EU approved medical ECG functionality, including background Afib detection – Includes skin temperature sensor – Supports Steps, Distance, Active Zone Minutes, VO2Max, Floor/elevation, Cardio Load, and many more metrics – Two sizes of bands (see specs below) – Water resistance level is 5ATM, and IP68 for dust protection

So that covers the piles of new stuff, and some of the bits that were there before. But there are still numerous color schemes/models to choose from.

The Fitbit Air case comes in 5 different colorways, and then with that, a huge slate of band options. Starting off with the core options you can buy, they are as follows:

– Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band – Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band – Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band – Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band – Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Stephen Curry Special Edition

From there, you’ve got the following band types/options:

– Active Band – Active Sport band – Metal Link band – Magnet band – Performance Loop

Now, for most of our testing (my wife and I), we’ve been wearing the relatively basic/default Active band, which works perfectly fine and is easy to adjust/etc.

Still, we both wore other bands as well. Yesterday we had a fancy afternoon thing to go to, and swapped out to the Metal Link band. Hers was the champagne gold, and mine the brushed silver. Obviously neither quite perfectly matched with the models we had, but…well…that’s the models we had:

My only complaint here is that I found the clasp release button could actually get reasonably easily pressed. Ironically, it didn’t happen all day during most of the day, and then towards the end of the day, it was triggering constantly. My wife didn’t have this issue, so….yeah.

I’ve also worn the Active Sport band a bit, though I didn’t honestly find it all that meaningfully different than the Active band, in terms of sport wearability.

And finally, I have the Magnet Band, which is super cool and just snaps tight/shut.

Finally, looking at the tech specs, here’s a whole slate of things that may or may not be interesting to you:

– Display is 1.34”/34mm AMOLED display, supporting an always-on configuration – Display supports adjustable brightness – Bluetooth 5.4 – Processor: Ambiq AP5 MCU – GPS chipset supports GPS+Galileo in US, and GPS+Galileo+GLONASS+BeiDou+QZSS outside of US – Onboard memory: 64MB NOR flash memory, 7 days of detailed motion data (minute intervals), 30 days of daily totals, heart rate at 2-second intervals – Internal sensors: Altimeter, Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Red and infrared sensors for oxygen saturation (SpO2), Multipurpose electrical sensors compatible with ECG app, Photoplethysmography (PPG) optical heart rate sensor, Ambient light sensor, Far-field skin temperature sensor – Battery is 65mAh – Fully end-user replaceable battery – Charging speed: 5 minutes of fast charging for 1 day of battery life, or 100% in 90 minutes – Requires iOS 16.4 or newer, and Android 11 or newer – Fitbit Edge Weight: 17.7g without band – Fitbit Edge Dimensions: 39.22 x 25.56 mm – Fitbit Edge Height/Thickness: 11.58mm – Case is made from 100% recycled aluminum – Active band: Silicone with “soft-touch coating” – Active Band Sizing: Small fits wrists 130-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around – Stephen Curry band: “Recycled polyester yarns with water-repellent coating and stainless steel lugs, as well as a raised interior print for increased airflow.” – Stephen Curry band sizing (US): Small fits wrists 135-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around – Stephen Curry band sizing (EU/Canada): Single-size fits wrists 150-195mm around – Water resistance: 5ATM/50 meters – Dust immersion resistance: IP68

Phew, got all that? Good, let’s roll right into the basics of the unit day to day.

In this section, I’ll go through all the daily usage basics of the Fitbit Edge, like activity/step tracking, sleep tracking, and general health bits. Then after this I’ll cover workout pieces.

First up is interacting with the device. The Fitbit Edge gained a physical button on the right side, which quickly opens the apps menu, for things like accessing the alarms, ECG, exercise, media controls, and weather. Previously on the Fitbit Charge 6, this was a touch-sensitive area, but not a clicking button:

The button is great, and I’ve been super happy with it. Note that at present, long-pressing it doesn’t do anything.

Instead, for most other interactions, you’ll use the touchscreen, which allows you to swipe left/right/up/down, and tap it for what you need. Of course, the first thing you’ll see is your watch face:
